opus-5.5.text:
I think the simplest way to put it is that for a long time the core of AI research was about inventing new methods and models. If you look at the most influential papers, things like AlexNet, the Transformer, GPT-3, they were mostly about a better way to train or a better architecture. Benchmarks mattered, but they played a supporting role. You'd build a benchmark, someone would come up with a new method that beat it by a few points, and that method was what got the credit. That was the game of the first half, and it worked really well.

What changed recently is that we finally have something like a working recipe. You take large-scale language pre-training, which gives you very strong priors, and you combine it with reasoning and acting, and then you do reinforcement learning on top. For years people thought the hard part of RL was the algorithm. But it turns out the priors and the environment matter much more. Once you have good priors from language, and the model can think before it acts, RL suddenly generalizes. The same recipe can climb software engineering, math, web browsing, computer use, without much task-specific trickery.

When that happens, the old game breaks. If one general recipe can hill-climb almost any benchmark you throw at it, then inventing a new method for one benchmark isn't that valuable anymore. The incremental method gets crushed by the next scaled-up general model. So the bottleneck moves. The interesting question is no longer "can we solve this benchmark," but "what should we be solving, and how do we measure real progress?"

And there's a gap that I think a lot of people feel. AI has beaten humans at chess and Go, gotten great at exams, olympiad-level problems, and yet the economy and everyday life haven't changed nearly as much as you'd expect. I call that a kind of utility problem. Part of the reason is that our evaluations don't look like the real world. They assume tasks are autonomous, the agent gets an input, does it alone, and gets scored. Real work involves interacting with people over time. They also assume tasks are i.i.d., each one independent, while in reality you get better at a job by accumulating experience, memory, context.

So to me the second half is about rethinking evaluation and problem definition, almost thinking like a product manager rather than just a researcher. Define new tasks that reflect real utility, then use the recipe, or improve it, to solve them. That's why it felt like an inflection point worth naming. The rules of the game have changed, and I think a lot of people are still playing the first-half game.

r001.rationale: The response describes a single working recipe that applies across software engineering, math, web browsing, and computer use, and says this changes the old game of task-specific methods.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the simplest way to put it is that for a very long time, maybe the past seventy years of AI, the hard part was methods. The bottleneck was: can we actually build a system that does this thing at all? Can it play chess, can it recognize images, can it hold a conversation, can it write code. So the game of the first half was, you propose a method, you pick a benchmark, you push the number up, and that's progress. And honestly that worked incredibly well. Most of the famous papers we cite are method papers, not benchmark papers.

What changed, in my view, is that we now have a recipe. Pretraining on language gives you a general prior, and then reinforcement learning on top of that, with reasoning and with real environments, lets you generalize that prior to new tasks. Once you have that, the loop becomes kind of mechanical. Someone proposes a benchmark, and within a few months the recipe eats it. Math olympiad, competitive coding, agent benchmarks, whatever it is. So the thing that used to be hard, getting a method that works, is no longer where the leverage is.

And that means the question flips. If the recipe works for almost anything you can define clearly, then the really hard question is: what should we define? What's actually worth doing? What's the environment, what's the reward, what does it mean for this to be useful in the real world? That's a problem of evaluation and problem formulation, and the field is honestly not very good at it, because we've been trained for decades to treat that as the boring part.

So I call it the second half because the rules of the game are different now. In the first half you win by solving problems. In the second half you win by finding the right problems, and by building evals that actually reflect utility instead of just being harder versions of the same exams. If we keep playing the old game, we'll keep saturating benchmarks that don't matter, and we'll be confused about why the world hasn't changed as much as the leaderboards say it should.

r001.rationale: The response describes a general recipe—language pretraining followed by reinforcement learning with reasoning and real environments—that applies across previously distinct tasks such as math, coding, and agent benchmarks, and identifies this shift as why the rules of the game changed.

astra-6.text:
I think we’re at an inflection point because the bottleneck is shifting. For a long time, the central question in AI was: can we train a model to perform a particular task? We would define the task, build a dataset, choose a benchmark, and improve the model. That work has produced increasingly general capabilities.

Now the question is becoming: how do we turn those capabilities into something useful in the real world? A model can do very well on a benchmark and still struggle to complete a project for you. It has to understand what you want, interact with an environment, recover from mistakes, and recognize whether it has actually succeeded. Those things aren’t captured very well by a single test score.

That’s why I use “Second Half.” It doesn’t mean model research is finished, or that we’re halfway to some predetermined destination. It means the emphasis is changing—from solving tasks that we’ve already formulated to figuring out which problems matter, how to formulate them, and how to evaluate whether an AI system has solved them. Better models remain essential, but the model alone is no longer the whole story.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shift from benchmark task performance toward real-world usefulness, problem formulation, and evaluation. It does not identify the emergence of one general method for solving AI tasks that were previously methodologically separate.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’re at an inflection point because the bottleneck in AI is shifting. For a long time, the central question was: can we train a model that performs well on a clearly defined task? You set up a benchmark, train a better model, and measure progress through a higher score. That approach has brought us very far.

But now, models can do many things reasonably well, and the harder question is: how do we turn those capabilities into something useful in the real world? A model might solve a difficult coding problem, but that doesn’t automatically mean it can take an ambiguous request, understand a large codebase, make the right changes, and verify that they actually work.

That’s the distinction I’m trying to capture with “Second Half.” The emphasis moves from solving a given problem to figuring out which problems to solve, how to define success, and how to build a system that can reliably reach that outcome. Evaluation becomes especially important, because in an open-ended environment, you don’t always have a clean answer key.

It doesn’t mean model training is finished or that scaling stops mattering. It means better models alone are no longer the whole story. More of the work—and more of the opportunity—is in connecting intelligence to real tasks and building the feedback loops that make it useful.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes a shift from benchmark performance toward applying models to useful real-world tasks, but does not identify one general method emerging to solve AI tasks that previously required separate methods.
